leads.text: In lib/sanitize.js:14, the guard `if (hasOwn(options,'allowedTags') && Array.isArray(options.allowedTags) && options.allowedTags.length > 0)` silently DISCARDS the strictest possible caller configuration, `allowedTags: []` ("allow no HTML tags at all"). Because the `.length > 0` clause is false for an empty array, line 15 `sanitizerOptions.allowedTags = options.allowedTags` never executes, so `sanitizerOptions` is handed to sanitize-html with no `allowedTags` key and the library reverts to its permissive built-in default tag allowlist. The protection the integrator explicitly requested is reverted to a weaker default with no error or warning. Blast radius is total: `initializeOptions(options)` at line 67 is the highest-centrality call in the whole graph (0.004966) and its result FLOWS_TO every sanitizeHtml sink (lines 37, 42, 57), so the downgrade applies to every sanitized value from req.body/params/headers/query.

leads.text: OBJECT KEYS ARE NEVER SANITIZED — only values are. In the object branch of `sanitize` (lib/sanitize.js:51-59) the walk is `Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { ... const item = data[key]; if (typeof item === 'string') { data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, options.sanitizerOptions); } else if (...) { data[key] = sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1); } })`. The loop variable `key` is read (to index `data`) and re-used verbatim as the destination property name, but is never itself passed through `sanitizeHtml` and the property is never renamed. An attacker POSTing `{"": "v"}` as JSON body, or sending `?

leads.text: Sanitizing `req.params` inside an application-level middleware is a no-op, leaving route parameters unsanitized. index.js:7 iterates `['body','params','headers'].forEach((k) => { if (req[k]) req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options); })`. When the middleware is mounted with `app.use(xss())` (the documented usage), Express has not yet matched a route, so `req.params` is an empty object — truthy, so the `if (req[k])` guard passes, but there is nothing to sanitize. Express's router then *replaces/populates* `req.params` with the matched route's parameters after this middleware has already run, so `req.params.id` and friends are delivered to the route handler completely unsanitized while the middleware reports success. Attacker-controlled path segments reach application output sinks un-neutralized.

Dependency query: express ^5.0.1.

leads.text: Attacker-triggerable unhandled exception / DoS via the depth limit. lib/sanitize.js:33-34 does `if (currentDepth > options.maxDepth) { throw new Error(`Maximum sanitization depth of ${options.maxDepth} exceeded`); }` with a default MAX_DEPTH of 100 (lib/sanitize.js:5). The throw happens synchronously inside the Express middleware (via the `Object.keys(data).forEach` callback at :51 and the `data.map` callback at :40), so a single POST whose JSON body nests objects/arrays more than 100 levels deep (e.g. `{"a":{"a":{...}}}`) aborts request processing with a 500 instead of rejecting or truncating the input. The middleware chooses to fail with an exception rather than degrade, and the limit is reached by ordinary attacker-controlled body nesting — cheap to send, repeatable, and it also prevents the request from ever being sanitized.

Recursion sites: line 45 "sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1)" (uid 98d222798df29cf02cf99ae786d5efd0f4032bc1, centrality=0.000656) and line 59 same (uid fef6a3baa5691710d96c30779838e0feeb5f738f). leads.text: FAIL-OPEN ALLOWLIST: `initializeOptions` only forwards `allowedTags`/`allowedAttributes` to sanitize-html when they are NON-EMPTY, so the two strictest configurations an integrator can express silently become the most permissive. At lib/sanitize.js:14 the guard is `hasOwn(options,'allowedTags') && Array.isArray(options.allowedTags) && options.allowedTags.length > 0`, and at :18 it is `hasOwn(options,'allowedAttributes') && Object.keys(options.allowedAttributes).length > 0`. An app that passes `allowedTags: []` (meaning "strip ALL HTML") or `allowedAttributes: {}` (meaning "allow NO attributes") fails both length checks, so `sanitizerOptions` is left WITHOUT those keys and is handed to `sanitizeHtml(data, options.sanitizerOptions)` at lib/sanitize.js:37/42/57 — where sanitize-html then applies its own built-in DEFAULT allowlist (which permits ``, ``, ``, ``, etc.) instead of stripping everything. The missing control is a distinction between "option absent" and "option present but empty"; the empty case must produce `allowedTags: []` explicitly rather than be dropped. Verifier should confirm by instantiating `xss({allowedTags: []})` and POSTing `hi` — the anchor is expected to survive.

'disallowedtags' OR 'transformtags' OR 'enforcehtml' OR 'allowedclasses' OR 'allowprotocolrelative' RETURN c.code  -->  row_count: 0 (no allowedSchemes / disallowedTagsMode / enforceHtmlBoundary ever passed through, so an integrator cannot compensate).

leads.text: NO UNCAUGHT-EXCEPTION GUARD AROUND THE DEPTH LIMIT — attacker-controlled nesting depth converts into a thrown Error on every request. `sanitize` throws unconditionally when the recursion exceeds the limit: lib/sanitize.js:33 `currentDepth > options.maxDepth` -> :34 `throw new Error(\`Maximum sanitization depth of ${options.maxDepth} exceeded\`)`, with the default `MAX_DEPTH = 100` (lib/sanitize.js:5) applying whenever the integrator does not pass `maxDepth`. Both call sites in the middleware — index.js:9 `req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)` and index.js:12 `const sanitizedQuery = sanitize(req.query, options)` — invoke it with no try/catch, and the strings 'try' and 'catch' appear nowhere in the scanned code. An attacker POSTing a JSON body nested deeper than 100 levels (cheap: a few KB of `{"a":{"a":...}}`) makes the middleware throw before `next()` at index.js:19, so the request is rejected/500s; because the middleware is typically mounted app-wide, any route reachable with a JSON body is affected. The missing control is catching the sanitizer's own error and converting it into a deliberate 400/413 rejection (or truncation) rather than letting it escape as an unexpected exception.

Query: ... c.line>=10 ... --> line 5: "const MAX_DEPTH = 100"; line 25: "hasOwn(options, 'maxDepth') && typeof options.maxDepth === 'number' && options.maxDepth > 0 ? options.maxDepth : MAX_DEPTH". leads.text: NO PROTOTYPE-POLLUTION KEY GUARD ON THE ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA WALK, despite the author having added one for the options object. `hasOwn` (lib/sanitize.js:7-9) deliberately uses `Reflect.ownKeys(object).filter(...)` rather than `in`/dot-access when probing `options`, showing the author guarded the CONFIG object against prototype-based key confusion. No equivalent guard exists on the untrusted data walk: lib/sanitize.js:51-59 iterates `Object.keys(data)` and performs raw `data[key] = ...` assignments with no denylist for `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`, and a graph-wide search for those literals returns nothing. Two sub-cases a verifier should check concretely: (a) a body parsed into a null-prototype object (Express 5's default 'simple' query parser / `Object.create(null)` containers) where `data['__proto__'] = ...` and `data['constructor'] = ...` assignments behave differently from plain objects; (b) `options.allowedKeys.includes(key)` at line 52 returning early, which skips a matching key's entire subtree unsanitized by design. Note the counter-argument that must be disproved: `JSON.parse` defines `__proto__` as an OWN data property, which shadows the `Object.prototype` setter and would make a plain `data['__proto__'] = v` a local write rather than a pollution — so this is reported as a missing guard to check, not a demonstrated pollution.

Contrast query (... c.line>=10 ...): line 8 "const keys = Reflect.ownKeys(object).filter((item) => typeof item !== 'symbol')" and line 9 "keys.includes(key)" — the hardened path, used only for `options` (hasOwn called at lines 14, 18, 23, 25).

leads.text: The depth-limit protection in lib/sanitize.js:33-34 throws synchronously (`throw new Error(...)`) and is invoked from the middleware's request handler (index.js:9 and 12) with no try/catch anywhere in either file, so a request body nested deeper than maxDepth (default MAX_DEPTH=100) converts the guard itself into an attacker-triggerable error path on every such request. The guard is also off-by-one relative to its own message (`currentDepth > options.maxDepth` permits maxDepth+1 levels), and its bound is caller-overridable via the same options object that lead 1 shows is parsed loosely.

leads.text: Runtime dependency `body-parser` is declared as `^1.19.0` in the manifest. The declared floor 1.19.0 predates body-parser 1.20.3, the fix for CVE-2024-45590 / GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (body-parser DoS via urlencoded `extended` parsing of requests with very many parameters), and body-parser 1.19.0's bundled `qs` 6.7.0 predates the qs 6.9.7/6.10.3 fix for CVE-2022-24999 (prototype-pollution/DoS). The pin is also stale on its face: it is declared alongside `express ^5.0.1`, and Express 5 bundles body-parser 2.x internally, so a 1.x direct dependency is an unmaintained leftover. Any committed lockfile resolving inside 1.19.x ships the vulnerable code; the caret only saves a fresh install. Verifier should check package.json + any lockfile for the resolved body-parser version.

Runtime deps present in the graph are body-parser ^1.19.0, express ^5.0.1, sanitize-html ~2.13.0.

leads.text: The single security-critical runtime dependency, `sanitize-html`, is pinned with a tilde range `~2.13.0`, which admits only 2.13.x and locks out every 2.14.x+ release. This package's entire XSS defense is delegated to sanitize-html: `require('sanitize-html')` at lib/sanitize.js:3 and the three `sanitizeHtml(data, options.sanitizerOptions)` sink calls at lib/sanitize.js:37, 42 and 57 are the only sanitization performed. sanitize-html has a recurring history of sanitizer-bypass advisories, so narrowing the range to one minor line means any upstream bypass fix published in a later minor is never picked up by `npm update` — the security boundary is frozen by a version literal. Verifier should confirm the tilde range in package.json and compare 2.13.0 against the current sanitize-html advisory list.

leads.text: The depth bound literal `const MAX_DEPTH = 100` (lib/sanitize.js:5) can be overridden by caller-supplied `options.maxDepth` with no upper bound: lib/sanitize.js:25 validates only `hasOwn(options,'maxDepth') && typeof options.maxDepth === 'number' && options.maxDepth > 0`, so values such as 1e9 or Infinity pass and replace the 100 default. `sanitize` recurses once per nesting level of attacker data at lib/sanitize.js:45 and lib/sanitize.js:59 (`sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1)`), and the data argument is attacker-controlled. With a large maxDepth configured, a deeply nested JSON body/query drives unbounded recursion into V8 stack exhaustion, crashing the worker (DoS). The guard literal is the only thing standing between attacker-controlled nesting depth and unbounded recursion, and it is user-overridable without a ceiling.

leads.text: The `MAX_DEPTH = 100` literal is enforced by an unconditional `throw` that an attacker can trigger at will: lib/sanitize.js:33-34 does `if (currentDepth > options.maxDepth) throw new Error(`Maximum sanitization depth of ${options.maxDepth} exceeded`)`. Because the middleware calls `sanitize()` synchronously inside a `forEach` callback (index.js:7-11) and again at index.js:12 for req.query, a request body nested more than 100 levels deep makes the middleware throw rather than sanitize. Two consequences: (a) attacker-forced 500 on any such request, and (b) the throw escapes mid-`forEach`, so of the `['body','params','headers']` keys only those processed before the throw are sanitized — remaining keys are left unsanitized on the req object if any caller catches the error and continues. The error message also reflects the configured maxDepth back to the client. The `throw` node is marked reachable from entry.

leads.text: The declared development toolchain is uniformly several majors behind and includes an end-of-life component: `eslint ^7.20.0` (the ESLint 7 line is end-of-life and no longer receives security support), `prettier ^2.2.1`, `chai ^4.2.0`, `supertest ^6.0.1`, `eslint-plugin-prettier ^3.3.1`, `eslint-config-prettier ^7.2.0`, `eslint-config-airbnb-base ^14.2.1`, `eslint-plugin-import ^2.22.1`. These are build/test-time only, so exploitability requires a malicious-repo or CI-supply-chain scenario rather than a request flow, but they are the components-with-known-vulnerabilities class and their transitive trees (notably ESLint 7's) carry unpatched advisories. Verifier should run an advisory audit against the resolved dev tree rather than trusting the declared ranges.
